## 1. Overview

This report models short-horizon and lifetime hard drive failure risk using a
2021-2022 sample of the Backblaze hard drive dataset (top 15 models by fleet
size, ~197k drives, ~127M valid drive-day observations), to inform third-party
hard drive insurance pricing. Four research questions are addressed with the
module's core methods - classification, time-series feature engineering,
clustering, and regression - with Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards
survival analysis used throughout as a supporting tool for handling censoring
and cross-validating the core-method findings. See `../README.md` for full
data provenance, pipeline documentation, and stated assumptions/limitations.

## 2. Data & Sample

```{r data-summary}
events <- load_events()
cat(sprintf("Drives: %d | Models: %d | Failures observed: %d (%.3f%%)\n",
            nrow(events), n_distinct(events$model), sum(events$failed),
            100 * mean(events$failed)))
```

The fleet is dominated by a small number of failures against a very large
population, consistent with hard drives being a genuinely reliable component
in aggregate - the central modelling challenge throughout this report is
extreme class imbalance, not lack of data volume.

## 3. Supporting Survival Analysis (Kaplan-Meier & Cox)

```{r km-overall, fig.cap="Overall Kaplan-Meier survival curve"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "km_overall.png"))
```

```{r km-model, fig.cap="Kaplan-Meier survival by model"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "km_by_model.png"))
```

```{r cox-summary}
cox_simple <- readRDS(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "cox_simple.rds"))
summary(cox_simple)
```

The baseline hazard is low and roughly flat over the short term (survival
probability at the 30-day mark, conditional on already having reached that
age, is ~0.997) - this is why RQ1/RQ2 use a **forward-looking 30-day failure
window** rather than raw age as the prediction target: age alone carries very
little short-horizon signal, so useful prediction has to come from SMART
attribute levels and trends. The Cox model shows large, statistically
significant hazard ratios across models (e.g. TOSHIBA MG08ACA16TE at ~8.6x
the reference model's hazard), confirming that **model identity is a strong
risk driver** in its own right and motivating the model-level comparisons in
RQ3/RQ4. The Schoenfeld residual test rejects strict proportional hazards
(expected at this sample size - even small time-varying deviations become
statistically significant), a caveat noted for the Cox-based projections in
RQ4.

## 4. RQ1 - Short-Horizon Failure Classification

*Can early-life SMART attributes predict whether a drive will fail within the
next 30 days, using a snapshot of its current SMART readings?*

```{r rq1}
rq1 <- readRDS(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "rq1_models.rds"))
cat(sprintf("Logistic regression AUC: %.4f\n", pROC::auc(rq1$roc_glm)))
cat(sprintf("Elastic-net logistic AUC: %.4f\n", pROC::auc(rq1$roc_glmnet)))
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "rq1_roc.png"))
```

Both classifiers substantially beat chance. The plain logistic regression
baseline (log1p-transformed, standardized, non-collinear raw SMART
predictors) reaches **AUC 0.85**, slightly ahead of the elastic-net model
(**AUC 0.79**) fit on the full raw+normalized attribute set - regularization
handles the collinearity in the fuller feature set well, but doesn't
outperform a carefully preprocessed simpler model here. This is a reasonable,
reportable result: SMART snapshots alone carry real short-horizon failure
signal, well above the ~50% chance line.

## 5. RQ2 - Value of Time-Series Features

*Do rolling time-series SMART features (7/30-day mean, volatility, and slope)
improve on snapshot-only prediction?*

```{r rq2}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "rq2_roc_comparison.png"))
```

Adding rolling features left ranking ability essentially unchanged (AUC 0.791
snapshot-only vs. 0.790 with time-series features added) but improved
precision-recall performance (PR-AUC 0.489 -> 0.509). Interpretation: a
drive's *current* SMART levels already capture most of the information needed
to separate failing from healthy drives in a 30-day window; the *trend*
information adds comparatively little extra ranking power, but does help
sharpen the precision/recall trade-off - useful for operational decisions
(e.g. setting an alert threshold) even though it doesn't move the headline
AUC much.

## 6. RQ3 - Degradation-Pattern Clustering

*Are there distinct clusters of drives with similar degradation trajectories,
and do they carry materially different failure risk?*

```{r rq3-clusters, fig.cap="Cluster scatter (PCA projection)"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "rq3_clusters.png"))
```

```{r rq3-km, fig.cap="Kaplan-Meier survival by cluster"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "rq3_km_by_cluster.png"))
```

```{r rq3-table}
rq3 <- readRDS(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "rq3_clustering.rds"))
knitr::kable(rq3$cluster_summary, digits = 4,
             caption = "Failure rate by degradation cluster (k=5, chosen by silhouette score)")
```

This is the strongest result in the report. K-means on rolling degradation
features (silhouette-selected k=5) separates drives into groups with failure
rates ranging from **~1.1% (largest, healthy cluster) up to 68.9% and 100%**
in two small, sharply distinct clusters - a difference of nearly two orders
of magnitude. The Cox score test (log-rank-equivalent, robust to the
left-truncated time axis used throughout) confirms the survival curves differ
across clusters far beyond chance (p < 0.001). Practically: unsupervised
degradation patterns alone, with no failure label used in fitting, recover
a highly actionable high-risk segment - exactly the kind of signal an insurer
would want for risk-based pricing tiers.

## 7. RQ4 - Expected Loss & Pricing Implications

*How does predicted failure risk translate into expected insurance losses
across drive models and coverage durations?*

```{r rq4}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "rq4_loss_curves.png"))
loss_table <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "rq4_loss_table.csv"))
knitr::kable(head(loss_table, 12), digits = 4,
             caption = "Expected loss by model and coverage length (head; cost proxy: $25/TB)")
```

Expected loss (failure probability from the per-model Cox survival curve,
times a capacity-based replacement-cost proxy) is well explained by coverage
length and model identity (R² = 0.81). Coverage length's linear/quadratic
terms are not individually significant once model is in the model - most of
the variation is *between models*, not within a model as coverage grows -
while several specific models (ST14000NM001G, ST12000NM0007,
TOSHIBA MG08ACA16TE) carry significantly higher expected loss than the
reference model at matched coverage length. This is the direct actuarial
takeaway: **a flat, fleet-wide warranty price would systematically
under-price some models and over-price others** - the model-level
differences here are large enough to justify risk-adjusted pricing tiers
rather than a single blended rate.

## 8. Discussion

**Summary of findings.** All four RQs point the same direction: hard drive
failure risk is predictable well above chance from SMART data (RQ1, AUC
0.85), the predictive signal is concentrated in current attribute *levels*
more than short-term *trends* (RQ2), degradation patterns cluster into
sharply different risk tiers even without using failure labels (RQ3, ~1% vs.
~70-100% failure rate), and that risk difference is large enough to matter
financially across models and coverage lengths (RQ4, R² = 0.81 with model
identity as the dominant driver). Together this supports a risk-segmented
approach to hard drive warranty/insurance pricing - by model at minimum, and
potentially by degradation cluster for finer-grained, usage-aware pricing.

**Limitations.**

- **Observational, enterprise-only population.** Backblaze operates data
  centre workloads; consumer usage patterns (temperature, vibration, power
  cycling) differ and these results should not be extrapolated to consumer
  warranty pricing without validation on consumer-representative data.
- **Reduced sample.** This analysis uses a 2021-2022, top-15-model subset of
  the full 2016-2022 Backblaze dataset (see `../README.md`) for tractability
  on commodity hardware; a production deployment would revisit that scoping.
- **SMART attribute coverage varies by manufacturer.** Feature engineering
  was restricted to attributes with broad cross-manufacturer coverage; some
  vendor-specific signal may have been left out.
- **Correlational, not causal.** SMART/degradation associations with failure
  are statistical associations from observational data, not causal effects.
- **RQ4's cost proxy ($/TB) is illustrative**, not real manufacturer or
  retail replacement pricing - the loss *curves and relative ordering* across
  models are the meaningful output, not the absolute dollar figures.
- **Cox proportional-hazards assumption is formally violated** per the
  Schoenfeld residual test (Section 3), likely reflecting real time-varying
  risk (e.g. infant-mortality vs. wear-out failure modes) rather than a
  modelling error; RQ4's loss projections should be read as first-order
  approximations, not precise hazard forecasts.
- **Left-truncation** is handled via power-on hours as the true age axis
  (robust to drives already in service before the observation window began),
  but drive removals for reasons other than failure (e.g. fleet migration)
  are not distinguishable from failure-free censoring in this dataset.

**Ethical and sustainability implications.** Risk-based pricing that
accurately prices in higher-failure-risk models could, if passed through to
manufacturers and consumers, create an incentive to discontinue or avoid
lower-reliability models - a plausible reliability-improving effect. It could
also concentrate replacement/e-waste incentives around specific models or
degradation signatures in ways worth monitoring, and predictive
"early-replacement" pricing signals raise a genuine tension between
minimizing warranty payouts and encouraging premature hardware replacement
(a sustainability cost) versus running drives closer to actual failure (a
data-loss risk). Neither is assessed quantitatively here, but both are live
considerations were this analysis to inform actual pricing policy.

## 9. Conclusion

SMART telemetry, engineered through standard analytics techniques
(classification, time-series features, clustering, regression) and
cross-validated with survival analysis, provides strong, actionable signal
for hard drive failure risk at a 30-day operational horizon and over full
warranty-length coverage periods. The clearest single finding is RQ3's
degradation clustering, which separates a small, unsupervised high-risk
segment carrying failure rates up to two orders of magnitude above the
fleet baseline - and RQ4 shows that risk difference is large enough, in
expected-loss terms, to justify moving away from flat, fleet-wide warranty
pricing toward risk-segmented pricing by model and/or degradation profile.
